assessment.name: Year 10 English Language Paper 1, Question 5 (creative writing)
assessment.sections: Monday 30 November, period 1. AQA English Language Paper 1 Question 5: write a description or a story, often from a picture. 40 marks.
assessment.weighting: Question 5 is 40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy. Reading questions 1 to 4 (homework weeks 2 to 4) are included here for the full paper later.

mock.note: 25 questions on the mark scheme, planning, structure and technical accuracy. Then write one Question 5 answer from the Written practice tab in 45 minutes.

units.name: The paper and the mark scheme

leitner_plan.quiz: Q5C quiz, then plan one story in 5 minutes
English mock (25), then one timed Question 5 (45 minutes)

cards.title: What Question 5 is
cards.question: What does Paper 1 Question 5 ask you to do, and how long should you spend?
points: You choose one of two tasks: describe something, or write a story. One task usually comes with a picture.
It is worth 40 marks, half of Paper 1. In the full paper spend about 45 minutes: 5 to 10 planning, 30 to 35 writing, 5 checking.
On Monday you have 50 minutes for Question 5 only, so you have time to plan and check properly.
The picture is a starting point. You can zoom in on one detail of it; you do not have to describe everything.
cards.watch_out: A description is not a story. If you choose the description task, you can show small changes, but do not build a long plot with lots of events.
cards.hook: 40 marks, 45 minutes: nearly a mark a minute.
cards.grade9: Pick the task you can make most original, not the one you think is easiest. Examiners reward a fresh angle on a simple idea.

cards.title: Content and organisation (24 marks)
cards.question: What does the examiner look for in the 24 content and organisation marks (AO5)?
points: Content: tone, style and register match the task and the purpose (to describe or narrate).
Ambitious, well chosen vocabulary and deliberate language devices.
Organisation: structural features used on purpose, such as a shift in focus or a cyclical ending.
Paragraphs that are linked and fluent, so the writing builds clearly.
Top band (19 to 24): compelling and convincing writing with varied and inventive structure.
cards.watch_out: Lots of devices crammed in does not score highly. The examiner wants devices that create a clear effect and feel natural.
cards.hook: Top band words to aim for: compelling, convincing, crafted.
cards.grade9: Every paragraph should earn its place. Before you write one, know what it adds: a new detail, a shift in mood, or a change in pace.

cards.title: Technical accuracy (16 marks)
cards.question: What earns the 16 technical accuracy marks (AO6)?
points: Sentence boundaries are secure: no comma splices, every sentence has a capital and a full stop.
A wide range of punctuation used accurately: commas, semicolons, colons, dashes, brackets, question marks.
A full range of sentence forms used for effect: short, compound, complex, minor sentences.
Standard English, accurate spelling including ambitious words, and extensive vocabulary.
cards.watch_out: One in every three marks for this question is for accuracy. Leave 5 minutes to proofread, because careless errors cost marks you have already earned.
cards.hook: SPaG plus range: spelling, punctuation, grammar, and show off a range.
cards.grade9: Use one semicolon, one colon and one set of brackets or dashes correctly, but only where they genuinely help the meaning.

cards.title: The four part plan
cards.question: What are the four parts of the story structure you have been taught, and what goes in each?
points: Setting: open with a precise, sensory picture of one place and time. Establish the mood.
Character: introduce one main character through actions, small details and thoughts, not a list of facts.
Change: something shifts, such as the weather, a sound, a discovery or a decision. This is the turning point.
Outcome: show the effect of the change on the character, then end with a link back or a strong final image.
Aim for about five or six paragraphs in total: one or two per part.

example.heading: Plan from the week 5 picture (people walking by a lake at sunset)
lines: Setting: the lake at dusk, the sky bruised orange, the water still.
Character: an old man walking his dog on the path he walked with his late wife.
Change: the dog runs into the shallows and finds her lost scarf, or the light disappears.
Outcome: he sits on their bench and watches the last light, calm at last. End on the water.

cards.watch_out: Do not plan too many events. One small change, written well, scores higher than a chase, an explosion and a twist.
cards.hook: Some Children Count Oranges: Setting, Character, Change, Outcome.
cards.grade9: Make the change emotional as well as physical. The weather can turn because the character's mood turns.

cards.title: Using the picture
cards.question: How do you turn a picture prompt into a strong plan?
points: List what you can see, hear, smell, touch and taste in the scene in 2 minutes.
Choose one small detail to zoom in on, such as a shadow, a hand, a reflection or a bird.
Decide whose eyes we see through and what they want or fear.
Pick a mood (calm, tense, lonely, hopeful) and choose words for that mood before you write.
cards.watch_out: Describing the picture left to right like a list reads as flat. Move the camera with a purpose: wide, then close, then wide again.
cards.hook: Five senses, one focus, one feeling.
cards.grade9: Use a symbol from the picture (the setting sun, a closed gate) and come back to it at the end so it gains meaning.

cards.title: Description or story
cards.question: What is the difference between the description task and the story task?
points: Description: the focus is a place or moment. Time moves slowly; you can show a small shift, such as before and after a storm.
Story: there is a character, a problem or change, and an outcome.
Both need a clear structure, a consistent viewpoint and a controlled ending.
The four part plan works for both. For a description, the change can be in the light, weather or crowd.
cards.watch_out: Dialogue in a description slows marks down. In a story, keep speech short and use it to reveal character, not to move the plot.
cards.grade9: A story can be told in a short time span, even five minutes. Narrow time lets you slow down and describe in detail.

cards.title: Openings that hook
cards.question: What are strong ways to open a Question 5 answer?
points: Start in the action (in medias res): begin in the middle of a moment, then explain later.
A short, striking sentence: The lake had swallowed the sun.
A sensory close up of one detail, before widening to the whole scene.
Avoid: It was a normal day. I woke up. My name is.

example.heading: Example opening
lines: Silence. Then the gulls, and the slap of small waves against the jetty.

cards.watch_out: Starting with the character waking up or a dream is common and predictable, so it rarely reaches the top band.
cards.hook: Drop the reader in the water, do not walk them to the pool.
cards.grade9: Hold back information. A question in the reader's mind (who is she waiting for?) keeps them reading.

cards.title: Moving the focus
cards.question: How can you use shifts in focus to structure your writing?
points: Zoom in and out like a camera: wide shot of the place, then a close up of one object or person.
Shift from outside to inside, or from the crowd to one person (as in the Cuckoo's Calling extract: the press, then the body).
Shift in time: present, a short flashback, back to the present.
Shift in mood: calm to tense, or tense to calm.
cards.watch_out: Every shift needs a signal for the reader: a new paragraph and a linking phrase such as Beyond the fence or Hours later.
cards.hook: Wide, close, wider: like a film camera.
cards.grade9: Write the shift so it creates contrast. The noisy crowd makes the silent body more shocking.

cards.title: Pace and paragraphing
cards.question: How do sentence length and paragraphs control pace?
points: Long, flowing sentences with lists slow the pace and build atmosphere.
Short sentences speed up the pace or create shock.
A one sentence paragraph gives a key moment impact.
Start a new paragraph for a new time, place, speaker, or a shift in focus or mood (TiPToP).
cards.watch_out: Too many one line paragraphs lose their power. Use one or two at turning points only.
cards.grade9: Match sentence length to the moment: slow at the calm start, quicker at the change, then slow again for the outcome.

cards.title: Endings
cards.question: How do you write an ending that feels crafted?
points: Cyclical ending: return to the opening image or line, but changed.
End on a strong, quiet image rather than an explanation.
A cliffhanger can work, but it must feel planned, not like you ran out of time.
Avoid: and then I woke up, or it was all a dream.

example.heading: Cyclical ending to match the opening
lines: Opening: The lake had swallowed the sun.
Ending: The lake gave nothing back. It never did.

cards.watch_out: Unfinished stories are capped. Plan the ending first so you always reach it.
cards.hook: End where you began, but changed.
cards.grade9: Use the final line to show how the character has changed without saying it directly.

cards.title: Viewpoint and tense
cards.question: How do you choose and control viewpoint and tense?
points: First person (I) gives closeness to thoughts and feelings.
Third person (he, she, they) lets you describe the character from outside and move around the scene.
Past tense is the usual choice. Present tense feels immediate and tense.
Choose one and keep it the whole way through.
cards.watch_out: Slipping between tenses (she walks, then she walked) is a common accuracy error that costs AO6 marks.
cards.grade9: Second person (you) or a change in tense for a flashback can work, but only if it is clearly deliberate.

cards.title: Show, do not tell
cards.question: What does show, do not tell mean, and how do you do it?
points: Telling names the emotion: He was nervous.
Showing gives evidence: His thumb worried at the frayed cuff of his sleeve.
Use actions, body language, small objects and the setting to reveal feelings.
Let the reader work out the emotion; this makes writing more convincing.
cards.watch_out: Lists of emotions (scared, sad and angry) read as telling. Pick one feeling and show it well.
cards.hook: Do not say the old woman screamed. Bring her on and let her scream. (Mark Twain)
cards.grade9: Use the setting to reflect the feeling, so emotion and place work together.

cards.title: Sensory description and pathetic fallacy
cards.question: How do you use the senses and the weather to build atmosphere?
points: Use all five senses, especially sound, smell and touch, which students often forget.
Pathetic fallacy: the weather or setting reflects mood. A storm for anger, mist for confusion.
Personification brings the setting to life: the wind clawed at the windows.
Choose precise nouns and verbs before you add adjectives.
cards.watch_out: Do not stack three adjectives on every noun. One precise verb (the fog swallowed the street) is stronger.
cards.hook: See, hear, smell, touch, taste: five senses, five chances.
cards.grade9: Build a semantic field (a group of linked words) such as decay: rotting, crumbling, rust, mould. It quietly creates mood.

cards.title: Figurative language
cards.question: Which figurative devices should you use, and how do you make them original?
points: Simile: comparing with like or as. Metaphor: saying one thing is another.
Extended metaphor: continue one comparison across a paragraph, such as the city as a sleeping animal.
Personification: give human actions to objects or nature.
Avoid clichés such as as quiet as a mouse; invent a comparison that suits your setting.

example.heading: Cliché to original
lines: Cliché: the sky was as black as coal.
Better: the sky had the colour of a bruise three days old.

cards.watch_out: A comparison must fit the mood. A cheerful image in a tense scene breaks the atmosphere.
cards.grade9: One extended metaphor that returns in the ending is more impressive than ten unrelated similes.

cards.title: Sound and word choice
cards.question: How can sound devices and ambitious vocabulary improve your writing?
points: Alliteration and sibilance (repeated s sounds) can create a soft or sinister tone.
Onomatopoeia gives sound effects: the clatter of plates, the hiss of the kettle.
Ambitious vocabulary: choose the most precise word, such as luminous, desolate, ominous, rather than nice or scary.
Contrast and juxtaposition: place opposites side by side, light and dark, noise and silence.
cards.watch_out: Do not use a long word you are unsure of. A wrong word loses marks and makes writing harder to follow.
cards.grade9: Vary vocabulary for the same thing (the lake, the water, the dark mirror) to avoid repetition.

cards.title: Sentence forms
cards.question: Which sentence forms should you use, and for what effect?
points: Simple: one clause. The door opened. Good for impact.
Compound: two clauses joined by and, but, or, so.
Complex: a main clause plus a subordinate clause, often starting with as, although, when, because.
Minor sentence: no main verb. Silence. Darkness. Use rarely, for effect.
Start sentences in different ways: with a verb ending in -ing, an adverb, a preposition or a subordinate clause.

example.heading: Varied openers
lines: Slowly, the tide crept in. Beneath the jetty, something moved. Although she was cold, she waited.

cards.watch_out: Starting most sentences with The or I looks repetitive and keeps you in the lower bands.
cards.hook: Start with -ly, -ing, a place or a when: four easy openers.
cards.grade9: Use a sentence fragment or a very long sentence once, deliberately, at the key moment.

cards.title: Punctuation range
cards.question: How do you use semicolons, colons, dashes and brackets correctly?
points: Semicolon joins two related full sentences: The lake was still; nothing moved.
Colon introduces a list, an explanation or a reveal: She saw it then: a hand.
Dashes or brackets add extra information: the old pier (closed for years) groaned.
Commas after a fronted phrase and around extra information: Beyond the trees, the sun sank.
cards.watch_out: A comma cannot join two full sentences. That is a comma splice. Use a full stop, a semicolon or a connective.
cards.hook: Semicolon: both sides must stand alone as sentences.
cards.grade9: Use an ellipsis or dash for a pause or interruption once, at the moment of tension, not throughout.

cards.title: Common accuracy errors
cards.question: Which spelling and grammar errors lose the most marks, and how do you avoid them?
points: their (belonging), there (place), they're (they are).
where (place), were (past of are), we're (we are); its (belonging), it's (it is).
should have, could have, would have, never should of.
Speech punctuation: new line for each new speaker, punctuation inside the speech marks.
Often misspelt: definitely, separate, necessary, silhouette, rhythm, environment, atmosphere.
cards.watch_out: Proofread for your own common mistakes. Most students repeat the same two or three errors.
cards.hook: Separate has a rat in it. Necessary: one collar, two sleeves (one c, two s).
cards.grade9: When proofreading, read each sentence on its own from the end backwards, so you see the words, not the story.

cards.title: Questions 1 and 2
cards.question: How do you answer Question 1 (4 marks) and Question 2 (8 marks) on Paper 1?
points: Q1: list four true things from the lines given. Short quotes or paraphrase are fine. About 5 minutes.
Q2: how does the writer use language? Words, phrases, devices and sentence forms. About 10 minutes.
Q2 paragraph: point, short quote, name the method, explain the effect, zoom into one word.
Use subject terms precisely: verb, adjective, simile, personification, sibilance.
cards.watch_out: In Q1 only use the lines given. In Q2 do not write about structure; that is Q3.
cards.hook: Q2 = What, How, Why: what the quote is, how it works, why the writer chose it.
cards.grade9: Explore more than one meaning of a word, as you did with tightly packed paparazzi suggesting both crowding and pressure.

cards.title: Question 3 structure
cards.question: How do you answer Question 3 (8 marks) on structure?
points: Track the focus and tone at the beginning, middle and end of the whole extract.
Use structure words: opens with, shifts to, zooms in on, contrasts, foreshadows, ends with.
Explain why the writer made each shift: to make the reader think, feel or ask something.
Your sentence starter: At the beginning of the extract the writer focuses on ... and there is a tone of ... Perhaps the writer wants to make the reader feel ...

example.heading: From your homework (The Cuckoo's Calling)
lines: Beginning: the press crowding the street, a chaotic tone.
Middle: shifts to a calmer, more composed tone.
End: the lifeless body and its injuries, a reflective but gory tone.

cards.watch_out: Do not analyse single words in Q3. You are marked on how the whole text is put together.
cards.hook: Beginning, middle, end: focus, tone, why.
cards.grade9: Comment on contrast between sections, such as the noise of the press against the silence of the body, and say what that reveals.

cards.title: Question 4 evaluation
cards.question: How do you answer Question 4 (20 marks), the evaluation question?
points: A student gives a view about part of the text. You say to what extent you agree.
Give your judgement at the start of each paragraph: I strongly agree that ...
Support with quotes and analyse language and structure methods.
Spend about 25 minutes. Write three or four developed paragraphs.

example.heading: From your homework (Mabel, Alaska 1920)
lines: Statement: the writer vividly conveys Mabel's sadness about losing her baby.
Evidence to use: the silence of the house, the absence of children, the lock of hair kept in a locket.

cards.watch_out: Q4 is not only language analysis. You must keep evaluating: how far the writer succeeds.
cards.grade9: Use evaluative verbs such as vividly conveys, powerfully suggests, and consider the reader's response.

cards.title: Question 5 checklist
cards.question: What must be in every Question 5 answer?
points: A 5 minute plan: setting, character, change, outcome, plus 6 ambitious words.
A hooking opening and a crafted, linked ending.
At least one clear shift in focus and one change in pace.
Show, do not tell; at least three senses; one original image.
Range: semicolon, colon, dash or brackets, varied openers, all accurate. Then proofread for 5 minutes.
cards.watch_out: Running out of time is the biggest risk. Look at the clock at 15, 30 and 40 minutes.
cards.hook: Plan, hook, shift, show, range, check.

written.q: Write a story inspired by the picture of people walking by a lake at sunset (homework week 5). 45 minutes. The marks below are a simplified guide to the 24 content and 16 accuracy marks.
model: Plan in 5 minutes using setting, character, change, outcome (2)
Opening hooks the reader, for example in medias res or a sensory close up (3)
Setting described with at least three senses and a clear mood (3)
Character revealed by actions and small details, showing not telling (4)
A clear change or turning point, with a shift in focus or pace (4)
Original imagery, such as an extended metaphor or pathetic fallacy (4)
Crafted ending, for example cyclical or a strong final image (4)
Sentence forms varied for effect, including varied openers (5)
Wide range of punctuation used accurately, including semicolon, colon, dash or brackets (5)
Accurate spelling, including ambitious vocabulary, and secure sentence boundaries (6)

written.q: Describe a busy street just after something dramatic has happened, as suggested by the Cuckoo's Calling extract. 45 minutes.
model: Plan includes a shift from wide scene to one detail and back (2)
Opening establishes the noise and crowd with sensory detail (3)
A clear shift in focus, such as from the crowd to a single person or object (4)
Description stays a description: little plot, time moves slowly (3)
Contrast or juxtaposition, such as noise against silence (4)
Precise verbs and a semantic field that build atmosphere (4)
Ending links back to the opening or ends on a powerful image (4)
Varied sentence lengths control pace (5)
Range of punctuation used accurately (5)
Accurate spelling and standard English throughout (6)

written.q: Write only the opening two paragraphs of a story titled The Storm. Then label the structural choices you made.
model: Opening line hooks, for example in medias res or a minor sentence (2)
Wide shot of the setting with sensory detail (2)
Second paragraph zooms in to a character or object (2)
Sentence length used to control pace (2)
Labels correctly name at least two structural choices (2)

written.q: Paper 1 Question 2 style: how does the writer use language to present the setting in the paragraph beginning Behind the tightly packed paparazzi? (homework week 2)
model: Clear point answering how the setting is presented, such as chaotic and intrusive (2)
Relevant short quotation, such as tightly packed paparazzi or teeming café (2)
Correct subject terminology, such as adjective, verb or juxtaposition (2)
Explains the effect on the reader and explores word level meaning (2)

exam_tips.timing: On Monday you have 50 minutes for Question 5. Plan 5 to 8 minutes, write 35, check 5. Look at the clock at 15, 30 and 40 minutes.
section_a: Read both tasks before choosing. Pick the one where you can picture one clear moment.
Plan setting, character, change, outcome and write the last line of your plan first.
Jot six ambitious words for your mood at the top of your plan.
section_b: Aim for five or six paragraphs. Quality beats length.
Show, do not tell. Use at least three senses.
Proofread for comma splices, tense slips and their, there, they're.
grade9: Zoom in on one moment and control the pace. A narrow scene written well beats a whole story rushed.
Change the mood only when something in the scene causes it, such as an announcement that silences a crowd.
Use one controlling image or symbol that returns at the end.
Make the structure deliberate, for example a flashback or a cyclical ending.
Choose the precise word, not the most impressive one. Rain needled the glass.
Use the full range of punctuation, but only where it helps the meaning.

mcq.q: How many marks is Paper 1 Question 5 worth?
mcq.e: It is half of Paper 1, which is 80 marks.

mcq.q: How many of the Question 5 marks are for content and organisation?
mcq.e: AO5 is 24 marks; AO6 technical accuracy is 16.

mcq.q: How many of the Question 5 marks are for technical accuracy?
mcq.e: AO6, spelling, punctuation, grammar and vocabulary, is 16 marks.

mcq.q: About how long should you spend on Question 5 in the full Paper 1?
mcq.a: 45 minutes
mcq.e: 40 marks, so about 45 minutes including planning and checking.

mcq.q: In Question 5, how many of the writing tasks do you answer?
mcq.a: One
mcq.e: You choose one of the two tasks.

mcq.q: Which describes top band content and organisation?
mcq.a: Compelling and convincing, with varied and inventive structure
w: Long, with lots of different devices
mcq.e: The top band rewards crafted, deliberate writing, not length or a twist.

mcq.q: Which of these is part of technical accuracy (AO6)?
mcq.a: A wide range of punctuation used accurately
mcq.e: AO6 is sentences, punctuation, spelling and vocabulary.

mcq.q: In the plan you were taught, what comes after Setting and Character?
mcq.a: Change
mcq.e: Setting, Character, Change, Outcome.

mcq.q: What is the Change in the four part plan?
mcq.a: The turning point that shifts the mood or situation
w: The last line of the story
mcq.e: The change is the moment something shifts, then the Outcome shows its effect.

mcq.q: Which is the best way to use a picture prompt?
mcq.a: Zoom in on one detail and build mood around it
w: Describe every object from left to right
mcq.e: A single detail and a clear mood make writing focused.

mcq.q: How long should you spend planning Question 5?
mcq.a: About 5 minutes
mcq.e: A quick plan saves time later and makes sure you reach the ending.

mcq.q: Which plan is most likely to score highly?
mcq.a: One small change described in detail
w: A chase, a fight and a twist ending
Five characters each with a backstory
A whole day from waking to sleeping
mcq.e: Fewer events give you space to craft language and structure.

mcq.q: What is a key difference between the description and the story task?
mcq.a: A description focuses on a place or moment; a story has a change and an outcome
w: A description must be in present tense
A story cannot describe the setting
mcq.e: Both need structure, but a description has little or no plot.

mcq.q: What does in medias res mean?
mcq.a: Starting in the middle of the action
mcq.e: It drops the reader straight into a moment.

mcq.q: What is a cyclical structure?
mcq.a: The ending returns to the opening image or idea
w: Every paragraph is the same length
Each section has a new narrator
mcq.e: Returning to the start, changed, makes the ending feel planned.

mcq.q: Which opening is most likely to hook the reader?
mcq.a: Silence. Then the slap of small waves against the jetty.
w: My name is Sam and I am fifteen.
I woke up and got ready for school.
mcq.e: A sensory, in the moment opening creates curiosity.

mcq.q: What does TiPToP help you remember?
mcq.a: When to start a new paragraph
mcq.e: New Time, Place, Topic or Person means a new paragraph.

mcq.q: What effect does a one sentence paragraph usually have?
mcq.a: It gives a key moment impact
w: It slows the pace right down
It shows the writer ran out of ideas
mcq.e: Isolating a sentence makes the reader pause on it.

mcq.q: What effect do long sentences with lists usually have?
mcq.a: They slow the pace and build atmosphere
mcq.e: Lists and clauses make the reader take in detail slowly.

mcq.q: Which ending should you avoid?
mcq.a: And then I woke up; it was all a dream
mcq.e: The dream ending undoes the story and feels unplanned.

mcq.q: What is a shift in focus?
mcq.a: Moving the reader's attention to a different place, person, time or detail
mcq.e: Shifts in focus are a key structural feature.

mcq.q: Which error in viewpoint or tense costs AO6 marks?
mcq.a: Slipping between past and present tense
mcq.e: Stay consistent unless a change is clearly deliberate.

mcq.q: Which sentence shows rather than tells?
mcq.a: His thumb worried at the frayed cuff of his sleeve.
mcq.e: Showing gives evidence through action instead of naming the feeling.

mcq.q: What is pathetic fallacy?
mcq.a: When the weather or setting reflects a mood
mcq.e: For example, a storm building as anger builds.

mcq.q: The wind clawed at the windows. Which device is this?
mcq.a: Personification
mcq.e: Clawing is a human or animal action given to the wind.

mcq.q: What is an extended metaphor?
mcq.a: One comparison continued across several lines or a paragraph
w: Two metaphors next to each other
mcq.e: Sustaining one image makes writing feel controlled.

mcq.q: What is a semantic field?
mcq.a: A group of words linked to one theme
w: A field described in a story
mcq.e: For example rotting, crumbling, rust and mould for decay.

mcq.q: Which is the strongest replacement for The fog was very thick and grey?
mcq.a: The fog swallowed the street.
w: The fog was extremely thick and grey.
The fog was thick, grey, cold and dark.
mcq.e: A precise verb is stronger than piling up adjectives.

mcq.q: What is sibilance?
mcq.a: Repeating s sounds
w: A word that sounds like its meaning
mcq.e: Sibilance can sound soft, secretive or sinister.

mcq.q: What is juxtaposition?
mcq.a: Placing contrasting ideas side by side
w: A word that imitates a sound
mcq.e: Noise beside silence or light beside dark creates contrast.

mcq.q: Which is a cliché that you should replace?
mcq.a: As quiet as a mouse
w: The sky had the colour of an old bruise
The lake had swallowed the sun
mcq.e: Clichés are overused and do not show originality.

mcq.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
mcq.a: The lake was still; nothing moved.
w: The lake was still; and quiet.
mcq.e: Both sides of a semicolon must be full sentences.

mcq.q: Which sentence is a comma splice?
mcq.a: The door opened, she stepped inside.
w: The door opened and she stepped inside.
As the door opened, she stepped inside.
The door opened. She stepped inside.
mcq.e: A comma alone cannot join two full sentences.

mcq.q: What is a minor sentence?
mcq.a: A sentence without a main verb, such as Darkness.
mcq.e: Minor sentences give dramatic emphasis.

mcq.q: Which is correct?
mcq.a: They're leaving their bags over there.
w: Their leaving there bags over they're.
There leaving their bags over they're.
They're leaving there bags over their.
mcq.e: they're = they are, their = belonging, there = place.

mcq.q: Which is correct?
mcq.a: I should have stayed.
mcq.e: Should have, could have, would have; of is never correct here.

mcq.q: Which word is spelt correctly?
mcq.a: definitely
mcq.e: Definitely contains the word finite.

mcq.q: Which sentence starts with a subordinate clause?
mcq.a: Although she was cold, she waited.
w: She waited although she was cold.
She was cold and she waited.
mcq.e: The subordinate clause comes first, followed by a comma.

mcq.q: What does a colon do in: She saw it then: a hand.
mcq.a: Introduces a reveal or explanation
mcq.e: A colon points forward to what follows.

mcq.q: How many marks is Paper 1 Question 1?
mcq.e: List four true things from the lines given.

mcq.q: Which question on Paper 1 is about structure?
mcq.a: Question 3
mcq.e: Q2 is language, Q3 structure, Q4 evaluation.

mcq.q: How many marks is Paper 1 Question 4?
mcq.e: The evaluation question is 20 marks; spend about 25 minutes.

mcq.q: In Question 3, what should you track through the extract?
mcq.a: The focus and tone at the beginning, middle and end
mcq.e: Q3 is about how the whole text is organised.

mcq.q: What must you do in every Question 4 paragraph?
mcq.a: Give a judgement on how far you agree, with evidence
mcq.e: Q4 rewards evaluation backed by analysis.

mcq.q: In Question 2, which of these should you NOT write about?
mcq.a: How the extract is structured
mcq.e: Structure is assessed in Question 3, not Question 2.

vocab.meaning: Suggesting that something bad is going to happen
vocab.example: The ominous clouds gathered over the lake.
The beach was desolate after the summer crowds had gone.
The luminous moon floated above the water.

vocab.meaning: A harsh mix of loud sounds
vocab.example: A cacophony of camera shutters filled the street.
The lake was serene until the dog splashed into it.

vocab.meaning: In a bad state because of age or neglect
vocab.example: A dilapidated jetty leaned into the water.

vocab.meaning: The dark shape of something against a lighter background
vocab.example: Her silhouette stood out against the orange sky.

vocab.meaning: A feeling that something bad will happen
vocab.example: A sense of foreboding settled over the empty house.

vocab.meaning: Placing two contrasting things side by side
vocab.example: The juxtaposition of the noisy crowd and the silent body shocks the reader.
The sunset was ephemeral, gone in minutes.
In the tranquil dawn, only the gulls called.
A quiet melancholy hung over the old man as he walked.
